stt: A C# Reading List by Eric Lippert
x:
I would put "CLR via C#" at the top of that list.  An absolutely necessary read for anyone using .NET

http://www.amazon.com/CLR-via-C-Jeffrey-Richter/dp/073562704...

There might be some optimizations on top of that, but overloadable operators in C# do get compiled to a function call (a static method call, if you want to be pedantic): http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6587107/c-sharp-operator-...

See VMAtm's comment's bytecode, showing that "[Decimal] + [Decimal]" compiles to:

    IL_0011: call    valuetype [mscorlib]System.Decimal [mscorlib]System.Decimal::op_Addition(valuetype [mscorlib]System.Decimal,
                                                                                              valuetype [mscorlib]System.Decimal)

Non-overloadable operators (short-circuiting operators (|| and &&), ternaries and its ilk, field access and (of course) the assignment operator) are probably compiled straight to bytecode, but they're pretty special and (especially in a strict language) need special runtime support anyway[0].

To sum up: mquander is completely right, the CLR does not know anything about operators, language compilers will take whatever operator they have at a high level and compile them to method calls (usually). For more details, see http://www.amazon.com/dp/0735627045/

[0] other runtimes make different choices, Python encodes most of its operators into bytecode for instance: http://docs.python.org/library/dis.html#opcode-BINARY_POWER
